images.title: Six sacks of 2 kg 500 g
images.purpose: Show that multiplying a weight multiplies both parts: 6 sacks of 2 kg 500 g make 12 kg and 3,000 g, which is 15 kg.
images.composition: A row of six equal sacks with their weight, three lines of working below, and the total in a box.
images.exact_structure: Plain white frame, 1456 by 816. SIX SACKS in one row at y 170 to 320, each a rounded rectangle 180 by 150 px filled amber #E69F00 with a 3 px dark outline and a tied neck 40 by 20 px on top, left edges at x 110, 325, 540, 755, 970, 1185, each holding the text 2 kg 500 g (34 px, bold, dark #1F2937). WORKING LINES centred at x 728 (44 px, bold, dark #1F2937): at y 430 the text 6 × 2 = 12 kg; at y 510 the text 6 × 500 = 3,000 g, which is 3 kg; at y 590 the text 12 kg + 3 kg = 15 kg. RESULT at y 700: a rounded rectangle 560 by 90 px centred at x 728 with a 4 px outline #0072B2 containing the text 15 kg in all (60 px, bold, teal #0072B2). Nothing else in the frame.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
any count of sacks that differs from 6
a sack with a weight other than 2 kg 500 g
images.takeaway: Multiply both the kg part and the g part, then exchange 1,000 g for 1 kg: 6 × 2 kg 500 g = 15 kg.
images.description: Six sacks of 2 kg 500 g with the working 12 kg plus 3 kg making 15 kg.
images.context: Concept image for Multiplying a Weight. It follows the idea of multiplying kg and g separately in your maths book and shows the concept's own example (practice values).
images.teaching_notes: Count the sacks, then multiply each part. The slip to watch: multiplying only the 2 kg.

image_decisions.why: Six equal sacks make the multiplication of both parts visible.
